1.pericope_label: Oh that my head were waters: oh that I had in the wilderness a lodging place of wayfaring men

schools.summary: Handles the idiom and the archaeology: the wish is put as a question, the fountain is a reservoir rather than a spring, and the lodging place is a caravanserai built on the route for travellers.

Explains why the prophet reaches for such extremity of language, being constrained to it by inflexible hearts, and reads the two charges as covering every defilement and a whole community consenting in its sins.

Brings eastern travel and pastoral experience to bear, the roofless shelter against wild beasts and the mean hut, and hears in the verse the voice of any minister who has preached long to a hardened people.
Finds a coincidence in the language, the same word serving for eye and fountain, and guards the wish from being read as a resolve to abandon the work.

debates.question: Does the opening verse belong to this chapter or to the one before it?

positions.view: it stands as the last verse of the preceding chapter in the Hebrew manuscripts and belongs there
it is closely tied to what precedes and even more closely to what follows, so that strictly there ought to be no break at all

debates.question: What is meant by calling them adulterers?

positions.view: metaphorically, all who had departed from God and were immersed in every kind of defilement, not the merely unchaste
adultery and faithlessness as the two cardinal sins, the second of conduct towards one's fellows rather than towards God
adulterers alike spiritually and literally

outliers.reading: Alone raises the question whether the wish is God's speech rather than the prophet's, reports that several interpreters take it so, and refuses the reading.
Alone guards the wish from being read as a plan, holding that the prophet had work he must not quit for his own ease and that we are not to go out of the world, bad as it is, before our time.

themes: Oh that my head were waters, and mine eyes a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people!
Oh that I had in the wilderness a lodging place of wayfaring men; that I might leave my people, and go from them! for they be all adulterers, an assembly of treacherous men.

3.pericope_label: They bend their tongues like their bow for lies: take ye heed every one of his neighbour

schools.summary: Restores the boldness of the metaphor, making the tongue itself the bow, corrects a proverbial mistranslation about valour for the truth, and catches the pun that turns every brother Israelite into a supplanter.

Divides on whether the warning is counsel or diagnosis, one voice reading it as advice against credulity and the other denying it is admonition at all and charging the people with being natural monsters.
Keeps the moral edge, naming the false prophets whose assurances left the people undefended and exclaiming at the drudgery by which men labour their way to ruin.

debates.question: Is the warning to beware one's neighbour advice, or a description of what is left?

positions.view: advice: do not be too credulous, keep clear of such company, since evil communications corrupt good manners
not an admonition at all, but a statement that no fidelity survived, charging the people with being natural monsters when even the worst usually keep some regard for kindred

debates.question: What does the word for the man who goes about among them mean?

positions.view: a slanderer; better rendered walketh a slanderer
not slander, which is too unmeaning here, but fraud: the word never appears without the verb to go, and describes one who moves about veiled seeking to cheat, its root being the word for a merchant

outliers.reading: Alone records his regret at correcting a phrase that had gained a proverbial character among champions of abstract right, since the Hebrew means only that they do not rule faithfully.
Alone identifies the lies concretely as the false prophets' assurance that no desolation was at hand, so that the people made no preparation and the sword destroyed them.

themes: And they bend their tongues like their bow for lies: but they are not valiant for the truth upon the earth; for they proceed from evil to evil, and they know not me, saith the Lord.
Take ye heed every one of his neighbour, and trust ye not in any brother: for every brother will utterly supplant, and every neighbour will walk with slanders.
And they will deceive every one his neighbour, and will not speak the truth: they have taught their tongue to speak lies, and weary themselves to commit iniquity.
Thine habitation is in the midst of deceit; through deceit they refuse to know me, saith the Lord.

7.pericope_label: I will melt them and try them: shall I not visit them for these things, saith the LORD

schools.summary: Reads the melting as a severer remedy after gentler ones failed, weighs the ambiguity of the preposition in the lament, and settles the identity of the creatures in the ruins as jackals rather than dragons.
Works the assayer's figure through, argues the geography against a people who thought the plains safe and the hills a refuge, and disputes the rendering of the verb describing the ruined pastures.
Names the instrument of the melting as the Chaldean war and supplies the natural history, the animal that follows the lion and devours what he leaves.

debates.question: What is the melting meant to accomplish?

positions.view: assay: as a goldsmith's furnace exposes copper passed off for gold, so hypocrites shine until they come to be really proved
the furnace of affliction, put to work to see whether the dross can be purged away
a severer remedy, the balm of Gilead having proved ineffectual against the disease
the fire of the Chaldean war, burning away the deceits they trust in so that a remnant may be purified

debates.question: Are the mountains and pastures burnt up, or desolate?

positions.view: desolate, so deserted that none pass over them; burnt up is an improper rendering
burned up, the prophet seeing himself upon the mountains and taking up the lament for them

outliers.reading: Alone stops to note that the future tense here stands for a present to mark a habitual practice, and remarks that the Welsh language continually does the same.
Alone reports that three of the versions turn the lament into an exhortation to others to take up a weeping, and holds instead that the prophet declares what he himself will do.

themes: Therefore thus saith the Lord of hosts, Behold, I will melt them, and try them; for how shall I do for the daughter of my people?
Their tongue is as an arrow shot out; it speaketh deceit: one speaketh peaceably to his neighbour with his mouth, but in heart he layeth his wait.
Shall I not visit them for these things? saith the Lord: shall not my soul be avenged on such a nation as this?

For the mountains will I take up a weeping and wailing, and for the habitations of the wilderness a lamentation, because they are burned up, so that none can pass through them; neither can men hear the voice of the cattle; both the fowl of the heavens and the beast are fled; they are gone.
And I will make Jerusalem heaps, and a den of dragons; and I will make the cities of Judah desolate, without an inhabitant.

12.pericope_label: Who is the wise man that may understand this: because they have forsaken my law which I set before them

schools.summary: Has sage and prophet alike asked in vain so that God answers himself, tidies an ambiguous clause about the deserted land, and identifies the bitter plant and the harder sense of the word for imagination.
Turns the unanswered question into a rule of wisdom and a claim of authority, closes the plea of ignorance by insisting the law was set before their face, and refuses the plant for plain bitterness.
Narrows the wise man to the one to whom God has revealed these things, reads the sentence as poison served in place of meat and drink, and alone qualifies how far the consuming went.
States the pastoral aim of the whole passage, to convince the people that they had brought the ruin on themselves and had no cause to quarrel with God.

debates.question: Who is the wise man that may understand this?

positions.view: nobody among them; the form of the question implies that no such man was to be found
the prophet alone, to whom God has revealed these things, as the fulfilment will show
sage and prophet are both called on and both fail, so that God answers himself through the prophet
hardly one in a hundred; and the question doubles as encouragement, since true wisdom is to consider God's judgments before he executes them

debates.question: Is the bitter thing they are fed wormwood?

positions.view: probably a species of Artemisia, four of which grow in the country, standing elsewhere for moral evil and here for the bitterness of calamity
not the plant, which is wholesome, but simply bitterness, since the word is never used in a good sense
poison served in place of meat and drink

outliers.reading: Alone turns the plea of inherited practice against his own age, denying that the example of the fathers can stand for law and holding that a long persistence doubles the crime instead of excusing it.
Alone qualifies the threat of consuming, observing that a full end was not in fact made and that only those appointed for destruction were consumed.

themes: Who is the wise man, that may understand this? and who is he to whom the mouth of the Lord hath spoken, that he may declare it, for what the land perisheth and is burned up like a wilderness, that none passeth through?
And the Lord saith, Because they have forsaken my law which I set before them, and have not obeyed my voice, neither walked therein;
But have walked after the imagination of their own heart, and after Baalim, which their fathers taught them:
Therefore thus saith the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel; Behold, I will feed them, even this people, with wormwood, and give them water of gall to drink.
I will scatter them also among the heathen, whom neither they nor their fathers have known: and I will send a sword after them, till I have consumed them.

17.pericope_label: Call for the mourning women: death is come up into our windows, and is entered into our palaces

schools.summary: Treats the wailing as a profession with its own art, corrects the clause that suggests the people left the land voluntarily, and rejects two rival constructions of the cry out of Zion.

Denies that the borrowed custom is endorsed, defends the hyperbole as not exceeding the vengeance coming, and reads the turn from hired women to women at large as the mark of a grief no money could supply.
Supplies the ethnography of hired mourning and reads the instruction to the daughters as a dirge meant to outlast the burial and pass down the generations.

debates.question: Does the prophet's use of the hired mourners endorse the custom?

positions.view: no: an absurd and foolish custom of almost every age, in which heirs bought feigned piety, and scripture often takes its similes from the vices of men
no: a foolish custom obtaining in most ages and countries, with its tearing of hair and beating of breasts
described without censure, as a trade with its own skill, the second class of women being called cunning because wailing was an art

debates.question: What is the death that comes up into the windows?

positions.view: the pestilence specifically, creeping in with its fatal taint while the invader is still held at bay
the assault itself, the enemy scaling the walls and breaking in at the tops of houses, with no respect to sex or age
death personified, entering suddenly like a thief in the night rather than because the doors are barred
a derision of men who supposed that closed doors could shut out God, whose power penetrates the thickest walls

outliers.reading: Alone traces hired mourning beyond the east to Ireland, where he says he has often witnessed it and supposes it was carried from the east, and derives the Greek and Phrygian practice from the Hebrew.
Alone catches what the summons implies, that the mourning women are called to the funeral not of a friend or a neighbour but of the nation.

themes: Thus saith the Lord of hosts, Consider ye, and call for the mourning women, that they may come; and send for cunning women, that they may come:
And let them make haste, and take up a wailing for us, that our eyes may run down with tears, and our eyelids gush out with waters.
For a voice of wailing is heard out of Zion, How are we spoiled! we are greatly confounded, because we have forsaken the land, because our dwellings have cast us out.
Yet hear the word of the Lord, O ye women, and let your ear receive the word of his mouth, and teach your daughters wailing, and every one her neighbour lamentation.
For death is come up into our windows, and is entered into our palaces, to cut off the children from without, and the young men from the streets.
Speak, Thus saith the Lord, Even the carcases of men shall fall as dung upon the open field, and as the handful after the harvestman, and none shall gather them.

23.pericope_label: Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom: but let him that glorieth glory in this, that he knoweth me

schools.summary: Places the saying as the climax of the whole prophecy, identifies the wise man as the recognised teacher, traces the verse into the apostle's hands, and reduces the doctrine to a sentence about where well-being comes from.
Insists the famous sentence is not a detached proverb but an answer to the confidence just rebuked, sorts the forbidden wisdom into its kinds, and explains why two words are used for knowing God.
Grounds the prohibition in God as the fountain of all good, sets a heathen poet beside the verse, and parcels the three attributes out to their proper objects.
Reads the three supports as the nation's war council, army and treasury, and asks for knowledge that retains its impressions rather than merely right apprehensions.

debates.question: Is the saying about glorying a detached proverb, or tied to what precedes?

positions.view: tied: it answers the confidence in prudence, defences and wealth just rebuked, and treating it as abruptly introduced diminishes much of its force
the climax of a long prophecy of judgment and the conclusion of the whole matter
aimed at the nation's boast of having wise men to advise the war, mighty men to fight it and rich men to bear its charges

debates.question: What wisdom is it that must not be gloried in?

positions.view: natural wisdom, the gifts that fit a man for public usefulness, and a speculative knowledge of gospel truths alike, none of which is grace
the scribe's: the wise man is the recognised teacher of the people
wisdom so called only by concession and common opinion, since the fear of God is the beginning of wisdom
any wisdom used as a shield against God, which is foolishness

outliers.reading: Alone sets a heathen poet beside the verse, quoting lines that tell the reader not to boast of wisdom or strength or wealth because one God alone is wise and mighty and rich indeed.
Alone assigns each of the three attributes its object: kindness as it relates to God's own people, judgment in punishing the wicked, righteousness in dealing justly with both.

themes: Thus saith the Lord, Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, let not the rich man glory in his riches:

But let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me, that I am the Lord which exercise lovingkindness, judgment, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, saith the Lord.

25.pericope_label: I will punish all them which are circumcised with the uncircumcised: all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in the heart

schools.summary: Corrects the English twice, first to circumcised in uncircumcision and then to the claim that all the heathen are uncircumcised in God's sight, and identifies the last group by a nickname of scorn.
Canvasses three constructions of the difficult phrase, explains the list by the alliances the Jews were counting on, and carries the argument forward to the boast of baptism without repentance.
Keeps the judgment even between Jew and Gentile, notes that the nations listed had been confederate against the same conqueror, and weighs the versions on the disputed epithet.

debates.question: How should circumcised with the uncircumcised be construed?

positions.view: circumcised in uncircumcision: all who have the outward sign without the inward purity it symbolised
three constructions are possible, and the best is that the mixture had made the rite indistinguishable from heathen uncircumcision, so the visitation falls on all without difference
Jew and Gentile alike feel the stroke, their transgressions being equal once advantages and disadvantages are fairly compared

debates.question: Who are those in the utmost corners?

positions.view: men in the farthest recesses, who think remoteness a safety; vengeance will reach into the corners where they suppose they dwell securely
those whose hair is cut short, following the ancient versions and the English margin
a wild tribe with the corners of their temples shorn, the epithet given in scorn like our round-head

outliers.reading: Alone charges the English version with making the prophet assert the exact opposite of what he said, since all the heathen are uncircumcised in God's sight whether they practise the rite or not.
Alone carries the argument into his own church, holding that to boast of baptism while destitute of repentance and faith is the same absurdity, the literal baptism availing hypocrites nothing.

themes: Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, that I will punish all them which are circumcised with the uncircumcised;

Egypt, and Judah, and Edom, and the children of Ammon, and Moab, and all that are in the utmost corners, that dwell in the wilderness: for all these nations are uncircumcised, and all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in the heart.
